article.title: The Republic on Trial
article.author: Peter McLaren
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On November 9, 2026, six days after the midterm elections, Donald Trump returned to a familiar accusation. Democrats had achieved what commentators were calling a blue tsunami, capturing control of both chambers of Congress and making substantial gains in states and districts that had long been regarded as Republican strongholds. Trump had initially indicated that he would accept the results. On election night, he told The New York Times that he was “absolutely willing” to do so. In an interview broadcast by CBS's 60 Minutes on November 8, he acknowledged the Republican losses and offered his explanation: he had not been on the ballot, and voters were unhappy with the economy and the war in Iran. The following day, however, he changed course. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” he wrote on Truth Social. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” The final sentence was particularly consequential. Trump did not identify a particular voting machine, produce evidence of altered ballots, or demonstrate that any machine had miscounted votes. But by invoking voting machines while questioning the honesty of the election, he again placed the integrity of the electoral process under suspicion. The accusation was not accompanied by evidence of widespread fraud or wrongdoing. Election officials had raised no major concerns about early voting or voting machines in the 2026 races. There was another problem with his complaint about the polls. Public surveys had broadly anticipated a Democratic wave. They had not necessarily predicted the full magnitude of the victories, but the direction of the results was hardly inexplicable. The electorate had delivered its judgment, and the available evidence did not substantiate Trump's insinuations about the machinery of the vote. The sequence is worth remembering. On election night, Trump said he would accept the results. Six days later, after the scale of the Republican defeat had become unmistakable, he questioned their honesty. Related: Trump, the Imperial Presidency, and the Perilous Future of the Republic This is not an isolated episode. It recalls a political pattern whose most consequential expression occurred after the presidential election of 2020, when Trump refused to accept defeat, advanced unsupported allegations of widespread fraud, and pursued an extraordinary effort to prevent the peaceful transfer of power. The calendar offers its own unsettling symmetry. On January 6, 2021, a violent crowd interrupted Congress's certification of Joe Biden's victory. On January 6, 2025, Congress peacefully certified Trump's own electoral victory. Now, in November 2026, the language of electoral suspicion has returned—not after a presidential defeat, but after the president's party suffered a sweeping midterm loss. To understand the significance of this moment, we must distinguish between changing votes and preparing to challenge an election; between legitimate scrutiny and unsupported allegations; between the right to contest a result and the obligation to accept evidence when the contest fails. The question is no longer confined to what happened in 2020, or what was prepared for in 2024. It concerns the durability of a republic in which the legitimacy of an election must not depend upon who wins. The Unfinished Business of 2020 The presidential election of November 2020 was followed not by a customary concession but by an escalating effort to reverse the result. Trump and his allies challenged results in battleground states, pressured state officials, promoted allegations of widespread fraud, and pursued legal strategies that failed in court. Recounts and audits did not substantiate claims of fraud sufficient to change the outcome. The effort extended beyond litigation. In several states, groups of Trump supporters signed certificates falsely purporting to represent legitimate presidential electors. These documents were part of a larger attempt to create an alternative account of the Electoral College vote. The pressure campaign also reached Vice President Mike Pence, whom Trump and his allies sought to persuade to reject or delay the certification of electoral votes. The congressional investigation into January 6 documented the extent of this effort. Its final report concluded that Trump's own campaign officials, Justice Department officials, and White House advisers had told him that his allegations of widespread fraud were false. Nevertheless, he continued to promote those allegations, pressured state officials to change certified results, and participated in efforts to transmit false electoral certificates to Congress and the National Archives. The report also documented Trump's pressure on Pence to refuse to count lawful electoral votes. Pence declined to do so. The constitutional significance of January 6, 2021, cannot be reduced to the violence of the Capitol attack, however shocking that violence was. The attack occurred within a broader political effort to obstruct the peaceful transfer of presidential power. The crowd that entered the Capitol interrupted the constitutional proceeding through which the result of the election was to be formally recognized. The courts rejected the principal legal challenges. State officials certified their results. Congress ultimately reconvened and completed the count. Yet the damage was not confined to the failed effort to retain the presidency. Trust in elections, public confidence in election administrators, and the security of those responsible for conducting elections had been placed under sustained pressure. The central lesson of 2020 was not merely that an attempt to overturn an election had failed. It was that the institutions of American democracy could be subjected to extraordinary pressure by a president unwilling to accept the judgment of the electorate. The Continuity of Personnel and Method The connection between 2020 and 2024 was not simply rhetorical. There were identifiable continuities in personnel and organizational practice. One particularly revealing example is Christina Bobb, a former Trump attorney who had been involved in efforts to challenge the 2020 election results, including the false-elector effort in Arizona. In March 2024, the Republican National Committee appointed Bobb as its senior counsel for election integrity. The Washington Post reported that Bobb remained in this position even after being charged in Arizona in connection with efforts to reverse the 2020 result. Her appointment was significant not because it proved that the 2024 election was to be manipulated, but because it demonstrated that a figure associated with the 2020 effort had moved into a prominent position within the party's formal election apparatus. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship The Republican Party was entitled to organize lawyers, recruit volunteers, monitor polling places, and challenge election procedures through the courts. Those activities are not inherently improper. Election integrity is a legitimate concern, and scrutiny of election administration is part of democratic accountability. But the political context mattered. Some of the people involved in the 2024 election operation had previously promoted claims about the 2020 election that were not supported by evidence. The organizational continuity deserved scrutiny, particularly when combined with the repeated suggestion that an unfavorable result could not be legitimate. The machinery of electoral distrust can be built without altering a single ballot. It can operate through public declarations, litigation, recruitment, political pressure, and the repeated suggestion that defeat is evidence of corruption. Preparing to Challenge the Result By the autumn of 2024, the Republican Party had assembled a substantial election operation. The campaign and the RNC pursued litigation over election rules and voting procedures, recruited volunteers to monitor elections, and prepared legal challenges that could be brought after the vote. Again, these activities must be described accurately. Filing lawsuits is not the same as falsifying votes. Poll watching is not inherently intimidation. Parties have a legitimate right to monitor the process and to seek judicial review when they believe election laws have been violated. The larger concern was the political context in which this operation developed. Trump repeatedly warned that the only way he could lose was through cheating. He urged supporters to deliver a victory “too big to rig,” while making unsupported allegations about noncitizen voting and other supposed avenues of electoral fraud. The effect of this rhetoric was to establish a political framework in which an unfavorable result could be treated as suspicious before the evidence had been examined. The distinction between rigging an election and preparing to contest its outcome is essential. The available record does not establish that the Trump campaign devised a plan to falsify ballots or alter the numerical outcome of the 2024 election. Trump won that election. The result was certified. But the preparations for legal and political challenges, when accompanied by repeated declarations that defeat could only result from cheating, raised a different question: Was the purpose merely to protect the integrity of the election, or was the public also being prepared to reject an unfavorable result? That question does not require us to assume that every lawyer or volunteer shared an improper purpose. It requires us to examine the documented statements, organizational relationships, and political conduct of those directing the operation. A democracy depends not only on the right to challenge an election, but also on the willingness to accept the outcome when the evidence does not support the challenge. The People Who Count the Votes The consequences of this political climate have been felt most directly by the people responsible for administering elections. A Brennan Center for Justice survey conducted in 2024 found that 38 percent of surveyed local election officials reported experiencing threats, harassment, or abuse because of their work. The survey also documented widespread concern about political interference and the safety of election workers and their families. These are not abstract constitutional concerns. Local election officials are the people who maintain registration records, supervise polling places, count ballots, certify results, and perform the often invisible work that makes representative government possible. Their independence is indispensable. When public officials and political leaders repeatedly cast doubt on election administration without evidence, the consequences reach beyond partisan disagreement. Election workers become targets. Some leave their positions. Others must consider the safety of their families. The ordinary administration of democracy becomes an act performed under intimidation. Related: Che Guevara, Paulo Freire, Cuba, and the Future of Hope A republic cannot function if the people who count its votes are expected to work under the threat of political retaliation. Nor can public confidence be restored simply by insisting that citizens trust the process. Trust must be sustained by evidence, institutional independence, transparency, and the willingness of political leaders to accept results they do not like. January 6, 2021—and January 6, 2025 The historical symmetry of January 6 is difficult to ignore. On January 6, 2021, Congress met to count the electoral votes confirming Joe Biden's victory. A violent crowd of Trump supporters stormed the Capitol, interrupted the proceedings, injured police officers, and threatened elected representatives and the vice president. The certification was delayed, but Congress eventually reconvened and completed its constitutional duty. Four years later, on January 6, 2025, Congress met again to certify the result of a presidential election. This time, Donald Trump had won. Vice President Kamala Harris presided over the proceeding and formally announced the result of her own defeat. Trump received 312 electoral votes; Harris received 226. No member of Congress objected to the results. The count was completed in approximately half an hour. The contrast was extraordinary. The candidate who had sought to overturn the previous election was now the beneficiary of a legitimate electoral victory. The candidate who had lost presided over the formal recognition of that victory. There was no violence, no mob, no interruption of the constitutional proceeding. The peaceful certification of 2025 was a necessary and welcome demonstration that the constitutional process could still function. But the contrast also raises a question that should not be evaded: Was January 6, 2021, an aberration, or did it reveal a vulnerability that remains unresolved? The peaceful proceedings of 2025 do not erase the events of 2021. Nor should the fact that Trump won in 2024 be used to retroactively validate the claims he made after losing in 2020. An election is not legitimate because the candidate whose victory was challenged eventually wins another one. Its legitimacy rests upon the rules, evidence, and constitutional procedures that govern every election, regardless of the identity of the victor. There was, however, an important institutional change between the two certifications. Congress passed the Electoral Count Reform Act in 2022, clarifying the vice president's limited role in the certification process and raising the threshold for congressional objections to a state's electoral votes. The law was intended to close vulnerabilities exposed in 2020. Such reforms matter. But legislation cannot by itself restore a political culture in which electoral defeat is accepted as part of democratic life. The law can establish procedures; it cannot compel political leaders to respect the principles that make those procedures meaningful. The Blue Tsunami and the Return of Electoral Suspicion The November 2026 midterms have added another chapter to this history. The Democratic victories were not confined to a handful of familiar battlegrounds. The party captured both chambers of Congress and made substantial gains across the country, including in states where Republican candidates had prevailed by considerable margins in 2024. The results produced a divided government and a new political reality for the remainder of Trump's presidency. A president is entitled to criticize election administration. He is entitled to request investigations, seek recounts, and present evidence of irregularities. The right to question government is not reserved for the opposition. Indeed, the credibility of democratic institutions depends upon their willingness to investigate genuine concerns. But allegations must be measured against evidence. Trump's November 9 statement did not identify a particular machine, jurisdiction, technical malfunction, or verified discrepancy. It did not offer evidence that votes had been altered. Election officials had not reported major concerns about the machines or early voting in the 2026 races. The public polling had broadly anticipated a Democratic wave, even if it had not fully captured its scale. The issue, therefore, is not whether election technology should be scrutinized. It should. Nor is it whether political leaders may challenge election procedures. They may. The issue is whether a president can repeatedly cast doubt upon the legitimacy of electoral outcomes without presenting evidence sufficient to support his accusations. When such claims come from the highest office in the country, they carry consequences. They can weaken public confidence in election administration, expose local officials to harassment, and encourage citizens to regard the counting of votes as a partisan enterprise rather than a constitutional responsibility. The 2026 statement also recalls the language of 2020. Then, Trump questioned the machinery of a presidential election he had lost. Now, after his party's midterm defeat, he has again invoked voting machines and questioned the honesty of the result. The circumstances are not identical. The 2020 effort involved a sustained campaign to reverse a presidential election, including pressure on state officials, false electoral certificates, and an attempt to obstruct congressional certification. The November 2026 statement, as of this writing, is a public allegation, not evidence of a comparable operational plan. We should not conflate the two. But neither should we ignore the recurring pattern: electoral legitimacy is called into question when the outcome is unwelcome. The Next Test: Congress and the Justice Department The midterm election has produced more than a change in congressional arithmetic. It has opened a confrontation over the constitutional authority of Congress to investigate the executive branch—and over the willingness of the administration to submit to that scrutiny. The conflict became unmistakable on November 7 and 8. As Democrats prepared to assume control of both chambers, President Trump denounced their proposed investigations as “extortion at the highest level.” He then went beyond public criticism. In a Truth Social post, he directed the Justice Department to investigate what he described as criminal conduct by Democratic lawmakers who had threatened investigations, impeachment, and other penalties against members of his administration. Attorney General Todd Blanche subsequently refused to rule out criminal investigations or prosecutions of Democratic lawmakers. On the Sunday political programs, he criticized their rhetoric and singled out Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat expected to chair the House Oversight Committee. Garcia had warned administration officials to “lawyer up” in anticipation of congressional inquiries. Related: Revolutionary Prophetic Pedagogy: Reclaiming Schools for Democracy in an Age of Oligarchy The details matter. According to Axios, Blanche did not identify a specific criminal statute that the lawmakers might have violated, nor did he confirm that the Justice Department had opened an investigation in response to Trump's directive. The Washington Post likewise reported that Trump had ordered the department to examine Democrats who had pledged to scrutinize his administration. The distinction between a presidential instruction, an actual investigation, and a prosecutable offense must be maintained. Nevertheless, the constitutional implications are serious. Congressional oversight is not, by itself, extortion or criminal conduct. It is one of the principal means by which the legislative branch holds the executive accountable. Congress has authority to investigate matters relevant to legislation, public expenditure, and the conduct of government. That authority is not unlimited, and individual lawmakers are not exempt from generally applicable criminal law. But the prospect of investigations, subpoenas, or impeachment proceedings cannot automatically be treated as criminal merely because the administration objects to them. The incoming Democratic majority has promised to examine a range of issues involving the administration, including its use of the Justice Department, its treatment of political opponents, immigration enforcement, and alleged conflicts of interest and corruption. Such inquiries will require evidence, procedural fairness, and discipline. Oversight must not become a substitute for proof, nor should impeachment be invoked as a partisan reflex. But the executive branch cannot claim immunity from investigation simply because the questions are politically inconvenient. The Washington Post reported on November 8 that the Justice Department was preparing for an extensive wave of congressional scrutiny after two years in which Republican congressional leaders had provided comparatively little oversight of the department's most contentious actions. Democrats are preparing subpoenas and investigative inquiries into the department's conduct during Trump's second term. The coming inquiries will examine, among other matters, the relationship between federal law enforcement and the White House. This confrontation is particularly consequential because the Justice Department occupies a position that demands institutional independence. Prosecutorial decisions should be grounded in evidence and law, not in the political interests or personal grievances of the president. When a president directs the department to investigate lawmakers who are preparing to investigate his administration, the appearance of a conflict between presidential interest and independent law enforcement becomes unavoidable. The administration has defended its position by arguing that lawmakers must not threaten private citizens, donors, or public officials with punishment simply because they hold opposing political views. Those concerns deserve examination where specific conduct is alleged. But the constitutional distinction remains: legitimate congressional oversight, including the investigation of executive officials and consideration of impeachment, is not rendered criminal by presidential objection. Here, the historical symmetry becomes difficult to ignore. After the 2020 election, Trump and his allies sought to enlist the Justice Department in efforts to challenge the result and retain presidential power. In the present confrontation, the department is being directed to examine lawmakers who intend to scrutinize the administration. The circumstances are not identical, and the facts must be assessed on their own merits. But in both episodes, the independence of federal law enforcement and its relationship to presidential power are central questions. The incoming Congress will have its own responsibilities. It must distinguish genuine misconduct from partisan accusation, protect the rights of witnesses, and ensure that investigations are grounded in evidence. It must also resist the temptation to turn oversight into spectacle. A congressional majority is not a license to presume guilt. But neither is the presidency a license to place the executive branch beyond scrutiny. The next test of constitutional government will therefore involve more than the conduct of elections. It will concern whether Congress can investigate the executive without intimidation, whether the Justice Department can exercise prosecutorial judgment independently, and whether the president can accept the constitutional limitations imposed upon his office. The republic's separation of powers was designed precisely for moments such as this. Its institutions are not supposed to protect those who hold power from accountability. They are supposed to make accountability possible. The Fragility of Democratic Consent The danger to democracy does not always arrive in the form of an unmistakable assault. Sometimes it develops through the gradual erosion of shared assumptions: that votes should be counted honestly, that evidence should matter more than accusation, that courts should be respected when they reject a claim, and that the peaceful transfer of power is not a privilege granted to the winning party but an obligation binding every participant. The events of 2020 demonstrated what can happen when those assumptions are abandoned. The preparations surrounding the 2024 election demonstrated how distrust could become embedded in a political organization's formal election apparatus. The peaceful certification of January 6, 2025, demonstrated that constitutional procedures can survive even after having been subjected to extraordinary strain. And the November 2026 statements and ensuing confrontation over congressional oversight have brought the question of constitutional accountability back into public view. These developments should not be collapsed into a single accusation. The 2024 election was not shown to have been stolen or falsified. Trump won it. The result was certified. The 2026 midterm results, too, have not been shown to involve widespread fraud or machine manipulation. Democrats won control of Congress. But the republic's health cannot be measured only by whether the machinery of government successfully completes its formal rituals. It must also be measured by whether political leaders respect the electorate when the electorate refuses them power; whether election officials can perform their duties without intimidation; whether Congress can exercise its oversight authority; and whether the Justice Department can distinguish the enforcement of law from the pursuit of political advantage. The issue is not whether a political leader who once challenged an election should be denied the opportunity to seek office again. The issue is whether the institutions of a republic can remain secure when the acceptance of electoral outcomes becomes conditional upon the identity of the winner. January 6, 2021, revealed the consequences of that condition in its most violent form. January 6, 2025, offered a moment of constitutional relief. November 9, 2026, reminds us that the underlying question has not disappeared. A republic is not sustained by the victory of one party over another. It is sustained by the willingness of those who lose to recognize that the people—not the president, not the party, not the movement—possess the final authority to decide who governs. And when the president himself questions the machinery by which the people have spoken, the burden is not on the electorate to prove that its voice was real. The burden is on the accuser to produce evidence. That principle is neither ceremonial nor negotiable. It is the unfinished business of American democracy. Selected Sources and Further Reading 1.
